passage:
"Chaitanya, look at your new bike!" Mummy clapped from the doorway. "You've earned it."
Pradeep, on the stairs, pressed his lips together. The last time he'd passed a class, nobody had bought anything.
Later, in the kitchen: "Mummy, can I say something? I'm happy for Chaitanya. Really."
"But?"
"But when he gets things, and you say well done, I feel like I'm not here. Last week I got picked for the debate team and you were on a call."
Mummy put the knife down. "I didn't know it felt like that."
"I'm not saying Chaitanya did anything wrong."
"No. He didn't." She touched his cheek. "Tell me about the debate."

qa.q: What did Pradeep get picked for last week?
qa.a: He got picked for the debate team.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling when he pressed his lips together on the stairs?
qa.a: He felt left out and invisible, as though his own efforts went unnoticed while his brother was celebrated.

qa.q: What did Pradeep do that gave his mother a chance to respond?
qa.a: He told her calmly what he noticed, said he was happy for his brother, and did not blame him.

qa.q: How might Mummy have felt when Pradeep explained?
qa.a: Probably surprised and a bit sorry, since she hadn't realised, which is why she put down the knife and asked about the debate. 🙂

grounding: Shows a teen watching his brother get gifts and praise, feeling invisible, and telling his mother without attacking the sibling.

passage:
The school auditorium was packed for Annual Day. Trisha's debate team had won the inter-house trophy that morning, but Mummy arrived only at four, just in time for Binita's Kathak.
From the third row, Trisha watched Mummy film every step of her sister's dance, eyes shining. At dinner last week Binita got new ghungroo. Trisha's torn debate folder was still taped together.
Backstage, Binita's ghungroo lay on a chair. For one ugly second, Trisha thought of sliding them under the curtain. She walked away instead, fists tight.
In the car she didn't sulk, though she wanted to. "Mummy, can I say something without it being about Binita?" Her voice wobbled. "Our team won today. You missed it. Lately I feel invisible."
Mummy was quiet at the red light. Then, "I didn't know about the trophy. Tell me about it now. All of it."

qa.q: What did Trisha's debate team win that morning?
What was Trisha feeling as she watched Mummy film Binita's dance?
qa.a: She felt envious and invisible, hurt that her own win was missed while her sister got every bit of attention.

qa.q: What went right in the car, and why?
qa.a: Trisha told Mummy what she noticed without blaming Binita, so Mummy could listen instead of defending her sister.

qa.q: How might Mummy see the conversation at the red light?
qa.a: She seems surprised and a little guilty, not having known about the trophy, and wants to make up for it by hearing the full story.

grounding: A teen who feels invisible beside her favoured sister resists hurting her and tells her mother what she notices without attacking the sibling.

passage:
Dear Papa,
I'm putting this on paper because when I try to say it, it comes out as a fight.
Raghav got the new phone in March. Raghav got to go on the Coorg trip with his friends. When Raghav cooks, you post a photo in the family group. When I made the whole Diwali rangoli, you said "nice" and went back to the news.
I'm not angry at Raghav. He didn't ask for any of it, and he lent me his headphones all last week. But I feel like I'm fading next to him, and it hurts more than I show.
I'm not asking for a phone. I'd like you to trust me with one trip, and notice when I do something I'm proud of.
Could we talk on Sunday, just us two?
Love,
Sharmila

qa.q: When did Raghav get the new phone?
How does Sharmila feel about the way Papa treats Raghav?
qa.a: Sharmila feels hurt and invisible, as if fading next to Raghav, while still feeling fond of him and not blaming him.

qa.q: What makes Sharmila's letter a good way to raise the problem?
qa.a: It gives clear examples, says plainly what Sharmila needs, and avoids attacking Raghav, which makes it easier for Papa to listen.

qa.q: How might Raghav feel if he read the letter?
qa.a: He might feel uncomfortable and a little guilty about the extra trust and praise, but glad that Sharmila does not blame him.

grounding: A teen envies the gifts and trust a brother receives and tells Papa plainly without attacking the sibling.
